title: Passive participles and impersonal sentences
objectives: I can form passive participles in '-ний', '-ений' and '-тий', decline them like adjectives, and name the doer of the action in the instrumental.
I can report a completed action with the forms in '-но' and '-то', keeping the object in the accusative, and an action in progress with a verb in '-ся'.
I can read signs, notices and short news items about buildings, monuments and opening hours.
I can say how I slept and what I feel like with impersonal sentences, and speak of a doer I do not name with the 'вони́' form.
I can explain the consonant changes and the stress of passive participles, and the 'і' that becomes 'о' in 'вхід', 'вхо́ду'.

vocabulary.note: 'Відчиню́', 'відчи́ниш', 'відчи́нять'. Imperfective partner 'відчиня́ти'. It is used for what swings open, such as a door, a window or a gate, and for a shop or a museum that opens at its usual hour. Passive participle 'відчи́нений'.
'Зачиню́', 'зачи́ниш', 'зачи́нять'. Imperfective partner 'зачиня́ти'. It is the opposite of 'відчини́ти' and is used for the same things. Passive participle 'зачи́нений'.

example.target: Окса́на зачини́ла две́рі й пішла́ на робо́ту.
example.source: Oksana closed the door and went to work.

vocabulary.note: 'Відкри́ю', 'відкри́єш', 'відкри́ють'. Imperfective partner 'відкрива́ти'. It opens anything (a book, a bottle, the eyes), opens something new to the public (a museum, a bridge, a café), and means to discover. Its opposite is 'закри́ти'. Passive participle 'відкри́тий'.

example.source: A new café has opened near the park.

example.target: У на́шому мі́сті буду́ють нову́ шко́лу.
example.source: They are building a new school in our town.
example.source_literal: In our city they-build new school.

vocabulary.note: Partner of 'будува́ти': 'збуду́ю', 'збуду́єш', 'збуду́ють'. Passive participle 'збудо́ваний', in which '-ува-' becomes '-ова-'.

example.target: Цей буди́нок збудува́ли за оди́н рік.
example.source: This building was built in one year.
example.source_literal: This building they-built within one year.

vocabulary.note: 'Засную́', 'заснує́ш', 'засную́ть', with the stress on the ending. Imperfective partner 'засно́вувати'. It is used for a city, a university, a company or a newspaper. Passive participle 'засно́ваний'.

Conjugated like 'да́ти', with the stress on 'ви-' in every form: 'ви́дам', 'ви́даси', 'ви́дасть', 'ви́дадуть'; past 'ви́дав'. Imperfective partner 'видава́ти' ('видаю́'). It publishes a book or a newspaper and issues a document. Passive participle 'ви́даний'.

example.target: Університе́т ви́дав нову́ кни́гу про Ки́їв.
example.source: The university has published a new book about Kyiv.

vocabulary.note: 'Ремонту́ю', 'ремонту́єш', 'ремонту́ють'. Perfective partner 'відремонтува́ти', passive participle 'відремонто́ваний'. It is used for buildings, apartments, streets and machines. The noun 'ремо́нт' means repair or renovation.

example.target: Сусі́ди ремонту́ють кварти́ру вже два мі́сяці.
example.source: The neighbors have been renovating their apartment for two months.
example.source_literal: Neighbors renovate apartment already two months.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'пам’я́тника'. It shares its root with 'пам’ята́ти', to remember. A monument to a person names the person in the dative.

example.target: Пам’я́тник Тара́сові Шевче́нку стої́ть у па́рку бі́ля університе́ту.
example.source: The monument to Taras Shevchenko stands in the park near the university.
example.source_literal: Monument to-Taras to-Shevchenko stands in park near university.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'собо́ру'. A cathedral is often named by an adjective made from the name of its saint: 'Софі́йський собо́р', Saint Sophia's Cathedral.

example.target: Ми ходи́ли в собо́р у неді́лю.
example.source: We went to the cathedral on Sunday.

vocabulary.note: A pause in work, in lessons or in opening hours. 'Зачи́нено на пере́рву' means 'closed for a break', with 'на' and the accusative of purpose.

example.target: На робо́ті в ме́не пере́рва о двана́дцятій.
example.source: At work I have a break at twelve.
example.source_literal: At work at me break at twelfth.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'вхо́ду'. It is built from 'в-', in, and the root of 'ходи́ти'. It names the door you go in by and also the right to go in: 'Вхід ві́льний.' (Admission is free.)

example.source: The entrance to the museum is from the street.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ви́ходу'. It is built from 'ви-', out, and the root of 'ходи́ти', and it also means a way out of a difficult situation.

example.source: The exit is on the left, by the elevator.

vocabulary.note: The form in '-но' of 'заборони́ти', the perfective partner of 'забороня́ти'. It never changes, and the sentence has no subject; what is forbidden is an infinitive or a noun in the accusative, and on signs it usually comes first: 'Пали́ти заборо́нено.' (No smoking; 'пали́ти' means to smoke.)

example.source: Entry to the bridge is forbidden.

vocabulary.part_of_speech: feminine noun, cited in the plural
vocabulary.note: The plural of 'нови́на', a piece of news. The news as a whole, and the news on radio or television, is 'нови́ни', with a plural verb and adjective: 'Які́ нови́ни?' (What's new?)
What a newspaper says is reported with the 'вони́' form and no subject: 'У газе́ті пи́шуть...' (The newspaper says..., literally 'in newspaper they-write').

example.source: My father reads the newspaper in the morning.

vocabulary.note: It is made from 'повідо́мити', to inform, with the suffix of 'оголо́шення' and 'ре́чення'. It is a message on a phone, a written notice, or a short report in the news.

dialogues.title: Closed for a break
dialogues.context: At one o'clock Sam and Oksana come to a museum in the center of Kyiv and find the door closed. They are friends and say 'ти'; with Bohdan, who works at the museum, they say 'ви'.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Окса́но, две́рі зачи́нені. Що тут напи́сано?
lines.source: Oksana, the door is closed. What does it say here?
lines.source_literal: Oksana, door closed. What here written?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Напи́сано: «Зачи́нено на пере́рву з пе́ршої до дру́гої».
lines.source: It says: 'Closed for a break from one to two.'
lines.source_literal: Written: «Closed for break from first to second».

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Пере́рва в музе́ї? Я ду́мав, що музе́ї працю́ють без пере́рви.
lines.source: A break at a museum? I thought museums were open without a break.
lines.source_literal: Break in museum? I thought, that museums work without break.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Не всі. А ось ще одне́ оголо́шення: «Фотографува́ти заборо́нено».
lines.source: Not all of them. And here's another notice: 'Taking photographs is forbidden.'
lines.source_literal: Not all. And here still one notice: «To-photograph forbidden».

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: До́брий день. Ви́бачте, у нас пере́рва. Ми відчи́нимо о дру́гій.
lines.source: Good afternoon. Sorry, we're on a break. We'll open at two.
lines.source_literal: Good day. Excuse, at us break. We will-open at second.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: До́брий день. А де вхід? Тут напи́сано «Ви́хід».
lines.source: Good afternoon. And where is the entrance? It says 'Exit' here.
lines.source_literal: Good day. And where entrance? Here written «Exit».

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Так, це ви́хід. Вхід право́руч, бі́ля пам’я́тника.
lines.source: Yes, this is the exit. The entrance is on the right, by the monument.
lines.source_literal: Yes, this exit. Entrance on-the-right, near monument.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Дя́кую. А в неді́лю ви працю́єте?
lines.source: Thank you. And are you open on Sunday?
lines.source_literal: I-thank. And on Sunday you work?

lines.speaker: Богда́н
lines.target: Працю́ємо. У нас зачи́нено в понеді́лок.
lines.source: Yes, we are. We're closed on Mondays.
lines.source_literal: We-work. At us closed on Monday.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Окса́но, що бу́демо роби́ти ці́лу годи́ну?
lines.source: Oksana, what shall we do for a whole hour?
lines.source_literal: Oksana, what we-will to-do whole hour?

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Мені́ ду́же хо́четься ка́ви. Ході́мо до Андрі́я?
lines.source: I really feel like a coffee. Shall we go to Andrii's?
lines.source_literal: To-me very wants of-coffee. Let's-go to Andrii?

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.target: Ході́мо. А о дру́гій пове́рнемося сюди́.
lines.source: Let's go. And at two we'll come back here.
lines.source_literal: Let's-go. And at second we-will-return here.

dialogues.title: News about the bridge
dialogues.context: On Saturday morning Taras visits his sister Olena. Her apartment is near the Dnipro, where a new bridge is being built, and Taras has brought a newspaper. They say 'ти'.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: До́брий ра́нок, Оле́но. Як тобі́ спало́ся?
lines.source: Good morning, Olena. How did you sleep?
lines.source_literal: Good morning, Olena. How to-you slept?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Пога́но. Мені́ всю ніч не спало́ся.
lines.source: Badly. I couldn't sleep all night.
lines.source_literal: Badly. To-me whole night not slept.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Чому́? Було́ галасли́во?
lines.source: Why? Was it noisy?
lines.source_literal: Why? Was noisy?

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Так. Уночі́ на мосту́ працю́ють, і там ду́же галасли́во.
lines.source: Yes. They work on the bridge at night, and it's very noisy there.
lines.source_literal: Yes. At-night on bridge they-work, and there very noisy.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ось у газе́ті пи́шуть про цей міст.
lines.source: Look, the newspaper has something about this bridge.
lines.source_literal: Here in newspaper they-write about this bridge.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Що пи́шуть? Прочита́й.
lines.source: What does it say? Read it to me.
lines.source_literal: What they-write? Read.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Слу́хай: «Нови́й міст че́рез Дніпро́ буду́ється вже два ро́ки».
lines.source: Listen: 'The new bridge across the Dnipro has been under construction for two years.'
lines.source_literal: Listen: «New bridge across Dnipro is-built already two years».

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Два ро́ки! А коли́ його́ закі́нчать?
lines.source: Two years! And when will they finish it?
lines.source_literal: Two years! And when it they-will-finish?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Тут напи́сано, що міст збудо́вано на сімдеся́т відсо́тків і його́ відкри́ють насту́пного лі́та.
lines.source: It says here that the bridge is seventy percent built and that it will be opened next summer.
lines.source_literal: Here written, that bridge built on seventy of-percent and it they-will-open of-next of-summer.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: А що ще пи́шуть?
lines.source: And what else does it say?
lines.source_literal: And what more they-write?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Ще одне́ повідо́млення: «У це́нтрі відремонто́вано пло́щу бі́ля собо́ру».
lines.source: Another report: 'In the center, the square by the cathedral has been renovated.'
lines.source_literal: Still one report: «In center renovated square near cathedral».

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Наре́шті! Її́ ремонтува́ли ці́лий рік.
lines.source: At last! They were renovating it for a whole year.
lines.source_literal: Finally! It they-renovated whole year.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Тобі́ хо́четься спа́ти? Відпочива́й, а я піду́ в магази́н.
lines.source: Do you feel sleepy? Have a rest, and I'll go to the shop.
lines.source_literal: To-you wants to-sleep? Rest, and I will-go to shop.

lines.speaker: Оле́на
lines.target: Дя́кую, Тара́се. Шко́да, що міст ще не збудо́вано!
lines.source: Thank you, Taras. It's a pity the bridge isn't built yet!
lines.source_literal: I-thank, Taras. Pity, that bridge still not built!

grammar.title: Passive participles: verb forms with adjective endings
grammar.explanation:
A participle is a form of a verb that takes the endings of an adjective. An adjective describes a noun by a quality ('нова́ кни́га', a new book); a participle describes it by an action. A passive participle describes the noun as the thing the action was done to: 'напи́сана кни́га' is a written book, a book that someone has written. English makes the same kind of word from most verbs ('written', 'opened', 'built') and never changes it. A Ukrainian participle agrees with its noun in gender, number and case, exactly as 'нови́й' does: 'напи́саний ро́зклад', 'напи́сана кни́га', 'напи́сане сло́во', 'напи́сані кни́ги', and in the locative 'у напи́саній кни́зі'.

Passive participles are made only from verbs that take a direct object in the accusative, because only such an action is done to something. Most come from perfective verbs, since they describe the result of one completed action. The participle is built on the infinitive with one of three suffixes, which end in the adjective ending '-ий':

- Verbs in '-ати' drop '-ти' and add '-ний': 'написа́ти', 'напи́саний'; 'прочита́ти', 'прочи́таний'; 'ви́дати', 'ви́даний'. Verbs in '-ува́ти' belong here and change '-ува-' to '-ова-': 'збудува́ти', 'збудо́ваний'; 'заснува́ти', 'засно́ваний'.
- Verbs in '-ити' replace '-ити' with '-ений', and the last consonant of the stem changes as it does in the 'я' form: 'зроби́ти' ('зроблю́'), 'зро́блений'; 'втра́тити' ('втра́чу'), 'втра́чений'; 'відчини́ти' ('відчиню́'), 'відчи́нений'.
- Some verbs with a short stem drop '-ти' and add '-тий': 'відкри́ти', 'відкри́тий'; 'забу́ти', 'забу́тий'; 'взя́ти', 'взя́тий'; 'поча́ти', 'поча́тий'. No rule picks out these verbs, so learn the participle with the verb.

A participle stands where an adjective stands. It can go before its noun ('зачи́нені две́рі', a closed door) or be the predicate, after a form of 'бу́ти' or, in the present, with no verb at all: 'Две́рі зачи́нені.' (The door is closed.) 'Музе́й був зачи́нений.' (The museum was closed.) Used this way, it describes a state that is the result of the action.

A participle with words of its own forms a participial phrase. The phrase usually follows its noun and is set off by commas: 'кни́га, напи́сана Окса́ною' (a book written by Oksana). The doer of the action, when it is named, is in the instrumental with no preposition, as if the person were the means of the action: 'Окса́ною', by Oksana. A participial phrase does the work of a relative clause with 'яки́й': 'кни́га, яку́ написа́ла Окса́на' means the same, and speech prefers the clause.

Ukrainian also has active participles, ending in '-учий' or '-ючий', which describe the noun as the doer of the action. Standard Ukrainian rarely uses them. Where English says 'the student reading a newspaper', Ukrainian uses a relative clause: 'студе́нт, яки́й чита́є газе́ту'. The few common words with these endings have become adjectives that name a lasting quality, such as 'співу́чий', melodious, from 'співа́ти': 'співу́ча мо́ва', a melodious language.

examples.source: This is a book written by Oksana.
The door is open, come in.

examples.target: Я купи́в кни́гу, ви́дану в Ки́єві.
examples.source: I bought a book published in Kyiv.
The museum was closed for a whole week.
Here is the student who is reading the newspaper.
The Ukrainian language is very melodious.

grammar.title: The forms in '-но' and '-то', and '-ся' for an action in progress
grammar.explanation:
The usual Ukrainian way to report that an action has been completed, without saying who did it, is an invariable verb form made from the passive participle: the participle's ending '-ий' is replaced with '-о'. 'Зро́блений' gives 'зро́блено', 'відчи́нений' gives 'відчи́нено', 'збудо́ваний' gives 'збудо́вано', and 'відкри́тий' gives 'відкри́то'. These forms in '-но' and '-то' are the predicate of a sentence that has no subject, and none can be added. They never change for gender, number or case.

The thing the action was done to stays the direct object, in the accusative, as in an active sentence: 'Робо́ту зро́блено.' (The work has been done, literally 'work done'.) English has to turn the object into a subject ('the work has been done'). Ukrainian leaves the subject empty and keeps the object, much as if it said 'someone has done the work'. Among nouns for things, the accusative differs from the nominative only in feminine nouns in '-а' and '-я', whose accusative ends in '-у' or '-ю': 'Кни́гу ви́дано.', 'Ву́лицю відремонто́вано.' For other things the accusative looks like the nominative: 'Музе́й відчи́нено.', 'Вікно́ відчи́нено.', 'Две́рі зачи́нено.'

The participle of the previous note agrees with a subject in the nominative and describes a state. Compare the two:

- 'Ву́лиця відремонто́вана.' The street is renovated: it is in that state now.
- 'Ву́лицю відремонто́вано.' The street has been renovated: someone has completed the work.

Both are correct, and often both translate the same English sentence. The form in '-но' or '-то' presents the event, and it is the usual choice in notices, news reports and official texts.

On its own the form reports a completed action whose result is present now, as English 'has been done' does. With a past time phrase it reports when the act happened, as English 'was done' does: 'Собо́р збудо́вано в одина́дцятому столі́тті.' (The cathedral was built in the eleventh century.) To mark the act explicitly as past, add 'було́', the neuter past of 'бу́ти'; to place it in the future, add 'бу́де', the 'він' form. Both take these forms because the sentence has no subject: 'Міст було́ збудо́вано за два ро́ки.' (The bridge was built in two years.) 'Міст бу́де збудо́вано насту́пного ро́ку.' (The bridge will be built next year.) 'Заборо́нено' works the same way with an infinitive: 'Пали́ти заборо́нено.' (Smoking is forbidden; 'пали́ти' means to smoke.)

These forms leave the doer unnamed, and they are used when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant. When the doer matters, say it in an ordinary active sentence: 'Окса́на зроби́ла робо́ту.' (Oksana has done the work.)

A form in '-но' or '-то' reports a finished result. For an action that is still in progress, Ukrainian uses an imperfective verb with '-ся', with the thing as its subject: 'Міст буду́ється.' (The bridge is being built.) 'Ву́лиця ремонту́ється.' (The street is being renovated.) This '-ся' has no reflexive meaning, since the bridge does not build itself; it shows that the subject undergoes the action. This construction never names the doer either. In conversation the 'вони́' form without 'вони́' is more common: 'Міст буду́ють.' (They are building the bridge.) The next note explains that form.

rows: The street was renovated in the summer.
The street will be renovated in the fall.

examples.source: All the books have been read.
The apartment has been renovated.

examples.target: Ки́ївський університе́т засно́вано в ти́сяча вісімсо́т три́дцять четве́ртому ро́ці.
examples.source: Kyiv University was founded in 1834.
examples.source_literal: Kyivan university founded in thousand eight-hundred thirty fourth year.

examples.target: Міст було́ збудо́вано за два ро́ки.
examples.source: The bridge was built in two years.
examples.source_literal: Bridge was built within two years.

examples.target: Нову́ шко́лу бу́де відкри́то у ве́ресні.
examples.source: The new school will be opened in September.
examples.source_literal: New school will-be opened in September.

examples.source: No smoking.
Our building is being renovated.

grammar.title: Impersonal sentences
grammar.explanation:
An impersonal sentence has no grammatical subject, and none can be added. You have met several kinds: predicative words, often with a person in the dative ('Мені́ хо́лодно.', 'Тобі́ тре́ба відпочива́ти.', and 'Було́ галасли́во.', it was noisy, from 'галасли́вий'), 'нема́є' with the genitive ('У ме́не нема́є ча́су.'), and the forms in '-но' and '-то' of the previous note. When the predicate of such a sentence is a verb, the verb takes the form that agrees with no subject: the 'він' form in the present and the future, and the neuter singular in the past, ending in '-ло'. This note adds three more kinds.

The first kind is a verb with '-ся' and the person in the dative. It names something that happens to the person, rather than something the person does:

- 'Мені́ не спи́ться.' (I can't sleep, literally 'to-me not sleeps'.) 'Я не сплю.' only states that I am awake. 'Мені́ не спи́ться.' says that sleep will not come, although I would like it to. The past is 'Мені́ не спало́ся.', and 'Як тобі́ спало́ся?' means 'How did you sleep?'
- 'Мені́ хо́четься ка́ви.' (I feel like a coffee, literally 'to-me wants of-coffee'.) What is wanted follows in the genitive or as an infinitive: 'Мені́ хо́четься спа́ти.' (I feel sleepy.) It names a wish you feel, and it is softer than the decision 'Я хо́чу ка́ву.' Its past is 'хоті́лося'.

The verbs 'спа́тися' and 'хоті́тися' are used only in the 'він' form and in the neuter past, and never with a person as subject.

The second kind names a process of nature with no subject at all, where English supplies an empty 'it': 'Надво́рі темні́є.' (It is getting dark outside.) The word 'надво́рі' means outside, and 'темні́ти', 'темні́є', means to get dark. The past is 'Надво́рі темні́ло.' Rain and snow are different, because there the noun is the subject: 'Іде́ дощ.'

The third kind uses the 'вони́' form of the verb without 'вони́'. It speaks of people in general, or of someone the speaker does not name, where English says 'they' or 'people':

- 'Тут не працю́ють у неді́лю.' (They don't work here on Sundays.)
- 'Ка́жуть, що за́втра бу́де дощ.' (People say it will rain tomorrow.)
- 'У газе́ті пи́шуть, що міст відкри́ють у тра́вні.' (The newspaper says the bridge will open in May.)

In speech this is the most common way to leave the doer out, more common than the forms in '-но' and '-то'. Adding 'вони́' changes the meaning: 'Вони́ тут не працю́ють.' speaks of particular people, 'they don't work here'.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: зро́блений, відчи́нено, збудо́вано, ви́дано
grammar.explanation:
A passive participle is built on the stem of its verb, so its spelling repeats the consonant changes and follows the stress of forms you already know.

The suffix '-ений' changes the last consonant of the stem exactly as the ending '-у' or '-ю' of the 'я' form does:

- After 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м' and 'ф' an 'л' is inserted: 'зроби́ти', 'зроблю́', 'зро́блений' [ˈzrɔblɛnɪj]; 'купи́ти', 'куплю́', 'ку́плений'.
- 'т' becomes 'ч': 'втра́тити', 'втра́чу', 'втра́чений'.
- 'с' becomes 'ш': 'запроси́ти', to invite, the perfective partner of 'запро́шувати', gives 'запрошу́' and 'запро́шений'.
- 'н' does not change: 'відчини́ти', 'відчиню́', 'відчи́нений'; 'заборони́ти', 'заборо́нений'.

The same inserted 'л' appears in the noun 'повідо́млення', made from 'повідо́мити', to inform, whose 'я' form is 'повідо́млю'. Its doubled 'н' before 'я' is one long soft consonant, [nʲː], as in 'життя́'.

In a participle from a verb in '-ити', the stress usually falls on the same syllable as in the 'ти' form of the verb: 'зро́биш', 'зро́блений'; 'ку́пиш', 'ку́плений'; 'відчи́ниш', 'відчи́нений'; 'заборо́ниш', 'заборо́нений'. Participles from verbs in '-ати' often move the stress one syllable toward the start: 'написа́ти', 'напи́саний'; 'прочита́ти', 'прочи́таний'. The form in '-но' or '-то' always keeps the stress of its participle: 'відчи́нений', 'відчи́нено'; 'відкри́тий', 'відкри́то'.

In verbs in '-ува́ти' the participle has '-ова-', and the stress falls on that 'о': 'збудува́ти', 'збудо́ваний', 'збудо́вано' [zbuˈdɔʋɑnɔ]; 'заснува́ти', 'засно́ваний'; 'відремонтува́ти', 'відремонто́ваний'. The present of the same verbs has '-у-': 'буду́ю', 'засную́', 'ремонту́ю', in which 'ю' after the vowel 'у' is [ju]. In 'збудо́вано' the 'з' of the prefix stays voiced before the voiced 'б'.

A perfective verb with the prefix 'ви-' is stressed on the prefix in every form, and so are its participle and its form in '-но': 'ви́дати', 'ви́дам', 'ви́дав', 'ви́даний', 'ви́дано' [ˈʋɪdɑnɔ]. The noun 'ви́хід' has the same stressed prefix.

The other new words follow the rules of the alphabet units:

- 'вхід', 'вхо́ду'; 'ви́хід', 'ви́ходу'; 'міст', 'мосту́': the 'і' of a closed last syllable becomes 'о' when an ending opens the syllable, as in 'кіт', 'кота́'. In 'мосту́' the stress also moves to the ending. In 'вхід' the 'в' before a consonant is said [w], and the final 'д' stays voiced.
- 'пам’я́тник' [pɑˈmjɑtnɪk]: the apostrophe after 'м' keeps the 'м' hard and the [j] sounded, as in 'м’я́со'.
- 'газе́та' [ɦɑˈzɛtɑ] has the voiced 'г' [ɦ], and the 'з' is hard before 'е'. In 'собо́р' both 'о' keep their full sound.
- In 'спи́ться' and 'хо́четься' the ending '-ться' is said [t͡sʲːɑ], as in 'прокида́ється'.
- In 'темні́є' the 'н' is soft before 'і', and 'є' after a vowel is [jɛ]. In 'надво́рі' the 'р' is soft before 'і'.
- 'Дніпро́', the river of Kyiv, is stressed on its last syllable, and the 'н' is soft before 'і'.
- 'Софі́йський' is stressed on 'фі', unlike the name 'Со́фія': an adjective in '-ський' can have a stress of its own.

The reading on the cathedral has two more forms in '-но':

- 'перебудо́вано', rebuilt, from 'перебудува́ти', 'будува́ти' with 'пере-' in the sense of again, with '-ова-' as in 'збудо́вано'
- 'збере́жено', preserved, from 'зберегти́', to preserve, whose 'я' form 'збережу́' changes 'г' to 'ж'; the participle 'збере́жений' repeats the change, as the participles in '-ений' do

culture.title: Signs, opening hours and the language of the news
culture.text:
Ukrainian shops, post offices, banks and museums put their opening hours on the door. Some of them close for an hour in the middle of the day, and the notice gives the time of the break: 'Пере́рва з пе́ршої до дру́гої'. Many museums are closed on one weekday, which the notice names.

Signs use the forms in '-но' and '-то' and other short phrases with no subject. These are the signs a visitor meets most often:

- 'Вхід' and 'Ви́хід', entrance and exit, and in the subway 'Ви́хід у мі́сто', the way out to the street
- 'Відчи́нено' and 'Зачи́нено', open and closed
- 'Зачи́нено на ремо́нт', closed for renovation
- 'Вхід ві́льний', admission is free
- 'Вхід заборо́нено', no entry
- 'Пали́ти заборо́нено', no smoking
- 'Обере́жно, пофарбо́вано!', wet paint, literally 'carefully, painted'
- 'Не працю́є', out of order, literally 'not works'

The same forms fill news reports and official texts, which state results without naming who achieved them: 'Відкри́то нови́й міст.' (A new bridge has been opened.) In conversation people retell the same news with the 'вони́' form and no subject: 'Відкри́ли нови́й міст.' Both are standard Ukrainian; the forms in '-но' and '-то' belong to the written style, and the 'вони́' form to speech.

Saint Sophia's Cathedral in Kyiv, 'Софі́йський собо́р', was built in the eleventh century and still keeps mosaics and frescoes from that time. In 1990 it became, together with the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, a monastery on the hills above the Dnipro, the first site in Ukraine on UNESCO's World Heritage List.

paragraphs.target: Сього́дні субо́та, і я ці́лий день гуля́в у це́нтрі Ки́єва. Я чита́в усі́ оголо́шення, які́ ба́чив, бо в них бага́то нови́х слів.
paragraphs.source: Today is Saturday, and I spent the whole day walking around the center of Kyiv. I read every notice I saw, because they have a lot of new words.
paragraphs.source_literal: Today Saturday, and I whole day strolled in center of-Kyiv. I read all notices, which I-saw, because in them many of-new of-words.

paragraphs.target: На по́шті я прочита́в: «Пере́рва з пе́ршої до дру́гої». Це означа́є, що о пів на дру́гу туди́ не ва́рто йти. А оди́н магази́н був зачи́нений, і на ньо́му було́ напи́сано: «Зачи́нено на ремо́нт».
paragraphs.source: At the post office I read: 'Break from one to two.' That means there is no point going there at half past one. And one shop was closed, and the sign on it said: 'Closed for renovation.'
paragraphs.source_literal: At post-office I read: «Break from first to second». This means, that at half to second there not worth to-go. And one shop was closed, and on it was written: «Closed for renovation».

paragraphs.target: У старо́му буди́нку, де живе́ мій друг Тара́с, я ба́чив оголо́шення «Ліфт не працю́є». Тара́с ка́же, що цей ліфт ремонту́ють уже́ три мі́сяці.
paragraphs.source: In the old building where my friend Taras lives, I saw the notice 'The elevator is out of order.' Taras says they have been repairing this elevator for three months already.
paragraphs.source_literal: In old building, where lives my friend Taras, I saw notice «Elevator not works». Taras says, that this elevator they-repair already three months.

paragraphs.target: А бі́ля музе́ю я прочита́в найкра́ще оголо́шення: «Сього́дні вхід ві́льний». Звича́йно, я пішо́в туди́. Фотографува́ти в музе́ї було́ заборо́нено, але́ я все до́бре запам’ята́в.
paragraphs.source: And near the museum I read the best notice of all: 'Admission free today.' Of course, I went in. Taking photographs in the museum was forbidden, but I remembered everything well.
paragraphs.source_literal: And near museum I read best notice: «Today entrance free». Of course, I went there. To-photograph in museum was forbidden, but I all well remembered.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer read every notice he saw?
choices: The notices have a lot of new words.
He was looking for the post office.
questions.explanation: The writer says 'бо в них бага́то нови́х слів', because there are many new words in them.

questions.prompt: What does the notice 'Пере́рва з пе́ршої до дру́гої' at the post office tell the writer?
choices: There is no point going there at half past one.
The post office opens at two in the morning.

questions.prompt: How long has the elevator in Taras's building been under repair?
questions.explanation: Taras says 'цей ліфт ремонту́ють уже́ три мі́сяці', with the 'вони́' form and no subject.

questions.prompt: Which notice did the writer like best?
questions.explanation: He calls it 'найкра́ще оголо́шення', the best notice, because admission to the museum was free that day.

paragraphs.target: Софі́йський собо́р стої́ть у це́нтрі Ки́єва. Це оди́н із найстарі́ших собо́рів Украї́ни. Будува́ти його́ поча́ли в одина́дцятому столі́тті, коли́ Ки́їв був столи́цею Ки́ївської Ру́сі.
paragraphs.source: Saint Sophia's Cathedral stands in the center of Kyiv. It is one of the oldest cathedrals in Ukraine. Its construction began in the eleventh century, when Kyiv was the capital of Kyivan Rus.
paragraphs.source_literal: Sophian cathedral stands in center of-Kyiv. This one of oldest of-cathedrals of-Ukraine. To-build it they-began in eleventh century, when Kyiv was by-capital of-Kyivan Rus.

paragraphs.target: У собо́рі збере́жено моза́їки й фре́ски одина́дцятого столі́ття. Ці моза́їки ба́чили лю́ди, які́ жили́ в Ки́єві ти́сячу ро́ків тому́.
paragraphs.source: Mosaics and frescoes from the eleventh century have been preserved in the cathedral. These mosaics were seen by people who lived in Kyiv a thousand years ago.
paragraphs.source_literal: In cathedral preserved mosaics and frescoes of-eleventh of-century. These mosaics saw people, who lived in Kyiv thousand of-years ago.

paragraphs.target: Наприкінці́ сімна́дцятого столі́ття собо́р перебудо́вано в сти́лі украї́нського баро́ко. Таки́м ми ба́чимо його́ й сього́дні.
paragraphs.source: At the end of the seventeenth century the cathedral was rebuilt in the style of the Ukrainian Baroque. That is how we still see it today.
paragraphs.source_literal: At-end of-seventeenth of-century cathedral rebuilt in style of-Ukrainian of-baroque. Such we see it and today.

paragraphs.target: У ти́сяча дев’ятсо́т три́дцять четве́ртому ро́ці в собо́рі відкри́то музе́й. Сього́дні його́ відві́дують лю́ди з усіє́ї Украї́ни й з і́нших краї́н.
paragraphs.source: In 1934 a museum was opened in the cathedral. Today it is visited by people from all over Ukraine and from other countries.
paragraphs.source_literal: In thousand nine-hundred thirty fourth year in cathedral opened museum. Today it visit people from whole Ukraine and from other countries.

questions.prompt: When did the construction of the cathedral begin?
questions.explanation: 'Будува́ти його́ поча́ли в одина́дцятому столі́тті.' The seventeenth century is when it was rebuilt, and 1934 is when the museum was opened.

questions.prompt: What has been preserved in the cathedral from the eleventh century?
questions.explanation: 'У собо́рі збере́жено моза́їки й фре́ски одина́дцятого столі́ття.' The Baroque look dates from the rebuilding at the end of the seventeenth century.

questions.prompt: What happened at the end of the seventeenth century?
choices: A museum was opened in the cathedral.
The cathedral was rebuilt in the Ukrainian Baroque style.
questions.explanation: 'Наприкінці́ сімна́дцятого столі́ття собо́р перебудо́вано в сти́лі украї́нського баро́ко.' The form in '-но' 'перебудо́вано' reports the rebuilding without naming who did it.

questions.prompt: In 'в собо́рі відкри́то музе́й', which word names the thing that was opened?
questions.explanation: 'Музе́й' is the object of 'відкри́то', in the accusative, which for a masculine thing looks like the nominative. 'В собо́рі' says where, and 'відкри́то' is the invariable form in '-то'.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian words with their meanings
Match the verbs with their meanings

pairs.source: to open a door or a window

choices: The bank is closed for a break.
The post office is closed for a break.
The post office is open after the break.
A noun made from a verb
A form of a verb with adjective endings that describes a noun as the thing an action was done to
A form of a verb that shows the person who acts
exercises.explanation: A passive participle such as 'напи́саний' takes the endings of an adjective and agrees with its noun: 'напи́сана кни́га', a written book.

exercises.prompt: Which word is the passive participle of 'зроби́ти'?
exercises.explanation: 'Зро́блений' has the suffix '-ений' and an adjective ending. 'Зроби́в' is the past form, and 'зро́блено' is the invariable form in '-но' made from the participle.

'Втра́тити' has 'т' becoming 'ч' in the 'я' form 'втра́чу', and the participle repeats it: 'втра́чений'. It agrees with 'ключ', masculine, in the accusative of a thing. 'Загу́блений', from 'загуби́ти', to lose ('загублю́'), is also correct.

exercises.hint_source: Oksana lives in a renovated building.
exercises.explanation: A participle declines like an adjective. 'Буди́нку' is a masculine locative after 'у', so the participle takes '-ому', as in 'у вели́кому буди́нку'.

exercises.prompt: In 'кни́га, напи́сана Окса́ною', what does the instrumental 'Окса́ною' show?
exercises.explanation: The doer of the action named by a passive participle is in the instrumental with no preposition. The person who receives something is in the dative, and an owner is in the genitive.

exercises.hint_source: Here is a book written by Taras.
exercises.explanation: The participle agrees with 'кни́га', feminine nominative singular, so it ends in '-а': 'напи́сана'. 'Тара́сом' in the instrumental names the doer.

exercises.prompt: How does standard Ukrainian usually say 'the student reading a newspaper'?
choices: With a relative clause: 'студе́нт, яки́й чита́є газе́ту'
exercises.explanation: Active participles in '-учий' and '-ючий' are rare in standard Ukrainian, which uses a relative clause with 'яки́й' instead.

exercises.audio_target: Цей собо́р збудо́вано в одина́дцятому столі́тті.
choices: This bridge was built in the eleventh century.
This cathedral was built in the twelfth century.
This cathedral was built in the eleventh century.

exercises.explanation: 'Робо́ту' is in the accusative, so the sentence has no subject and the predicate is the invariable form in '-но'. With the nominative 'робо́та' the participle would agree: 'Робо́та зро́блена.'

exercises.prompt: Which word completes '___ відремонто́вано.' (The school has been renovated.)?
exercises.explanation: With a form in '-но' the thing the action was done to stays the object, in the accusative: 'Шко́лу відремонто́вано.' The nominative 'шко́ла' would need the participle: 'Шко́ла відремонто́вана.'

exercises.hint_source: The street will be renovated in the fall.
exercises.explanation: 'Бу́де' places the form in '-но' in the future. It is the 'він' form because the sentence has no subject; 'було́' would place it in the past.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says that the bridge is being built right now?
exercises.explanation: An imperfective verb with '-ся' presents an action in progress. 'Міст збудо́вано.' reports the finished work, and 'Міст збудо́ваний.' describes the bridge as built.

exercises.hint_source: The new library is still being built.
exercises.explanation: The building is still in progress, so the imperfective 'будува́ти' takes '-ся' and agrees with the subject 'бібліоте́ка': 'буду́ється'.

choices: 'Л' is the sign of every passive participle.
The 'л' comes from the past form 'зроби́в'.
After 'б', 'п', 'в', 'м' and 'ф' the suffix '-ений' inserts an 'л', as the 'я' form 'зроблю́' does.
exercises.explanation: The suffix '-ений' changes the stem as the 'я' form does: 'зроблю́', 'зро́блений'; 'куплю́', 'ку́плений'. Participles such as 'відчи́нений' and 'ви́даний' have no 'л'.

choices: On 'ви-', because a perfective verb with the prefix 'ви-' is stressed on it in every form
On 'да', because a form in '-но' moves the stress
On 'но', because the ending is stressed
exercises.explanation: 'Ви́дати', 'ви́дам', 'ви́дав', 'ви́даний' and 'ви́дано' are all stressed on 'ви-'. A form in '-но' keeps the stress of its participle.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Мені́ не спи́ться.' say that 'Я не сплю.' does not?
choices: That sleep will not come, although I would like to sleep
exercises.explanation: With '-ся' and the dative, the sentence presents sleep as something that happens to the person. 'Я не сплю.' only states that I am awake.

exercises.hint_source: Do you feel like some tea?
exercises.explanation: 'Хо́четься' takes the person in the dative, 'тобі́', and the thing wanted in the genitive, 'ча́ю'. The sentence has no subject.

exercises.prompt: In 'Тут не працю́ють у неді́лю.', who does not work on Sundays?
choices: Particular people the speaker has named
The people of this place, whom the speaker does not name
exercises.explanation: The 'вони́' form without 'вони́' speaks of people in general or of a doer the speaker does not name. 'Вони́ тут не працю́ють.' would speak of particular people.

exercises.prompt_target: У газе́ті ___, що нови́й музе́й відкри́ють восени́.
exercises.hint_source: The newspaper says the new museum will open in the fall.
exercises.explanation: What a newspaper says is reported with the 'вони́' form and no subject, literally 'in newspaper they-write'.

choices: They say the cathedral will be repaired in the spring.
They say the monument will be repaired in the spring.
They say the monument will be repaired in the fall.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, why can't Sam and Oksana go into the museum?
choices: It is Monday, and the museum is closed.
The museum is closed for a break until two.
The museum is closed for renovation.
exercises.explanation: The notice says 'Зачи́нено на пере́рву з пе́ршої до дру́гої', and Bohdan says 'Ми відчи́нимо о дру́гій.' The museum is closed on Mondays, but this is not a Monday.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, why couldn't Olena sleep?
choices: She was reading the news all night.
People were working on the bridge at night, and it was noisy.
exercises.explanation: Olena says 'Уночі́ на мосту́ працю́ють, і там ду́же галасли́во.'

exercises.prompt_source: Where is the way out to the street here?
I'm reading a book published in Lviv.

exercises.hint_source: The museum is open from ten.

exercises.explanation: The form in '-но' reports the closing as an act; the participle 'зачи́нений' describes the museum's state. Both are correct, and so are the same forms of 'закри́ти', 'закри́то' and 'закри́тий'.
'Відкри́то' is the form in '-то' of 'відкри́ти', with 'міст' as its object. In speech the 'вони́' form 'відкри́ли' without 'вони́' says the same.
'Хо́четься' takes the person in the dative and an infinitive. The sentence has no subject; 'мені́' may be left out when the speaker is obvious.
